question: In Italy, there is an increasing number of farms at risk of closure due to the EU’s new energy strategy. The latest case concerns the province of Vercelli, in Piedmont, where no less than 420 hectares of rice fields that have been part of the landscape for more than 400 years are about to be expropriated to make space for new agro-photovoltaic and photovoltaic parks for foreign multinationals such as Morgan Stanley.

This situation is a clear distortion of the European market caused by foreign multinationals, which, in addition to the steadily shrinking amount of arable land due to green policies, only aggravates the situation in the Italian and European agricultural world. According to estimates, compared to 20 years ago, the number of farms managing 38% of the EU’s land has gone from 15 million to 9.1 million.

In light of the above, given that as much as 50% of the national agricultural production comes from the Vercelli area alone, and that these energy projects would, furthermore, lead to the loss of almost 30 000 quintals of rice each year: 1.
Can the Commission say how it intends to intervene so that the affected farms get the support they need?
How does it intend to protect the European market from such activities, which directly result in dependence on imports from outside the EU, given the loss of food production?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.2.2024) According to information received from the Piedmont regional authorities, the expropriation concerns the cable ducts and not the land for installation of solar panels. Compensation for expropriations is provided for in national legislation.
The Commission is aware of land constraints associated with competition for space and recognises the importance of balancing the need to ensure both food and energy security.

This is why the EU Solar Energy Strategy, adopted in May 20221, puts emphasis on rooftop deployment and on the development of solar installations that promote multiple use of space, including agrivoltaic systems, where energy production and agricultural activities take place simultaneously on the same area.

Under the EU legal framework, and in particular Article 4(4) of Regulation (EU) 2021/21152, direct payments under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) are paid for agricultural land that is predominantly used for an agricultural activity3, provided that certain other conditions are met.

In case non-agricultural activities, such as energy production with solar panels, are also exercised on the land, Member States must define in their CAP Strategic Plans under which conditions an agricultural activity is considered to be predominant. Moreover, the Italian CAP Strategic Plan for the 2023-2027 period provides for coupled income support for agricultural land cultivated with rice.
Solar energy panels must be installed in compliance with national and EU legislation.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and
Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions EU Solar Energy Strategy https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?

uri=COM%3A2022%3A221%3AFIN&qid=1653034500503 2 Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 of The European Parliament and of the Council of 2 December 2021 establishing rules on support for strategic plans to be drawn up by Member States under the common agricultural policy (CAP Strategic Plans) and financed by the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) and by the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1305/2013 and (EU) No 1307/2013.
3 The definition of agricultural activity is specified in Article 4(2) of Regulation (EU) 2021/2115.
